front_blocks.md: What are **halogens**?

back_blocks.md: **Halogens** are the Group 7 elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine. They are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules at room temperature and become progressively darker in colour going down the group.

cards.front_md: What are **halogens**?

front_blocks.md: What is a **halogen displacement reaction**?

back_blocks.md: A **halogen displacement reaction** is a reaction in which a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

cards.front_md: What is a **halogen displacement reaction**?

front_blocks.md: What is a **disproportionation reaction**?

back_blocks.md: A **disproportionation reaction** is a reaction in which the same species is simultaneously both oxidised and reduced.

cards.front_md: What is a **disproportionation reaction**?
cards.back_md: A **disproportionation reaction** is a reaction in which the same species is simultaneously both oxidised and reduced.

front_blocks.md: Why does the reducing power of halide ions increase going down Group 7?

back_blocks.md: Going down the group, the halide ions become larger and have more electron **shielding**. Their outer electrons are held less tightly by the nucleus, so it is easier to lose electrons, making larger halide ions stronger **reducing agents**.

front_blocks.md: Define **volatility**

back_blocks.md: **Volatility** is how easily a substance evaporates. A more volatile substance has a lower boiling point.

front_blocks.md: What colour change is seen when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?

front_blocks.md: What type of compound is formed when a halogen reacts with a Group 1 or Group 2 metal?

back_blocks.md: An **ionic** compound called a **metal halide salt** is formed. In these reactions the metal is always **oxidised** and the halogen acts as the **oxidising agent**.

front_blocks.md: What is observed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium chloride?

back_blocks.md: **Misty fumes** of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas are produced. No further reaction occurs because Cl<sup>-</sup> is a weak reducing agent and cannot reduce the sulfuric acid further.

front_blocks.md: Why do the boiling points of the halogens increase going down Group 7?

back_blocks.md: Going down the group, the halogen molecules have more electrons, so **London dispersion forces** between molecules become stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point increases.

back_blocks.md: Iron is oxidised from Fe<sup>2+</sup> to **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>. Both chlorine and bromine are strong enough **oxidising agents** to bring about this change.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Iodine can oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Iodine is not a strong enough **oxidising agent** to oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>. In fact, iron(III) ions oxidise **iodide ions** to iodine, not the other way around.

back_blocks.md: Halogens are more **soluble** in the organic layer than in the aqueous layer. This makes the colour changes easier to observe, helping to identify which halogen has been produced.

front_blocks.md: In the displacement of bromine by chlorine, which species is oxidised and which is reduced?

back_blocks.md: **Bromine** is oxidised: Br goes from -1 to 0. **Chlorine** is reduced: Cl goes from 0 to -1. The reaction is therefore a **redox** reaction.

front_blocks.md: What products are formed when chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH (around 15°C)?

back_blocks.md: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH to form **NaCl** and **NaClO** (sodium chlorate(I)). This is a **disproportionation** reaction: chlorine is reduced to Cl<sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to −1) and oxidised to ClO<sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to +1).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

Fluorine is the smallest halogen with the least electron shielding. Its nucleus attracts incoming electrons most strongly, making it the most powerful **oxidising agent** and the most reactive halogen.

front_blocks.md: Why does the oxidising power of halogens decrease down Group 7?

back_blocks.md: Going down the group, atomic radius increases and there is more electron **shielding**. Incoming electrons are attracted less strongly by the nucleus, so each halogen is less able to gain an electron and act as an **oxidising agent**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Bromine can displace chloride ions from potassium chloride solution.

Bromine is less reactive than chlorine. Only a **more reactive** halogen can displace a less reactive one. Bromine can only displace iodide ions, not chloride ions.

front_blocks.md: Write the ionic equation for the displacement of iodide ions by bromine.

back_blocks.md: Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → 2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) + I<sub>2</sub> (aq)

front_blocks.md: How does chlorine make drinking water safe?

back_blocks.md: Chlorine reacts with water to form **chloric(I) acid** (HClO), which kills **bacteria** and acts as a sterilising agent. HClO can also dissociate to form ClO<sup>-</sup>, which is also a sterilising agent.

front_blocks.md: Why must reactions of halide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid be carried out in a fume cupboard?

back_blocks.md: The reactions produce **toxic gases** such as HCl, HBr, SO<sub>2</sub>, and H<sub>2</sub>S. A fume cupboard prevents these harmful gases from escaping into the laboratory.

front_blocks.md: Why can silver nitrate not be used to test for fluoride ions?

back_blocks.md: **Silver fluoride** (AgF) is **soluble** in water, so no precipitate forms. This is an exception to the general trend for silver halides, which are insoluble.
